title: Own the Graph: Stephen Costigan on Private AI, Knowledge Infrastructure, and Law Firm Advantage
author: Stephen Costigan

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s copilot framing by retaining lawyer judgment while shifting work from assembly to editing. However, it does not address whether automating first-draft production weakens junior expertise development or whether deliberate training, mentorship, simulation or independent practice is needed to compensate.
qs: Stephen Costigan (15:00)  What I mean is that the system is not there to replace a lawyer’s judgment.
The lawyer spends time editing and deciding, not assembling.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Costigan raises AI ownership as a possible organisational choice, which is relevant to the cluster’s unresolved architecture question. But the excerpt does not explain whether ownership improves adaptation, human control, performance or economics, so it does not establish a clear position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: I am happy to talk with any firm thinking about owning its AI rather than renting it.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Costigan accepts the cluster’s core framing of agentic AI as connected workflow delegation with continuing lawyer oversight. He materially extends it by describing adversarial model review before a cited first draft reaches the lawyer and private infrastructure intended to govern sensitive data, while offering product claims rather than measured evidence of reliability or security.
qs: At a high level, we give the lawyer a first draft that has already been argued against by a second, adversarial system.
Stephen Costigan (15:00)  What I mean is that the system is not there to replace a lawyer’s judgment.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source accepts that realized AI value depends on organisational adoption rather than tool acquisition alone, and materially extends the cluster by proposing two concrete enablers: firm-owned knowledge infrastructure that preserves control, and leadership practices that give users agency to change how they work. Its product and adoption claims remain experience-based rather than independently validated.
qs: I’ll start by saying our platform turns a firm’s documents and matter history into a private, curated knowledge graph that the firm owns and runs inside its own environment.

I think it is a good thing for leaders to remember at this time, and something for all of us to remember as we encourage people to change the way they work and adopt new technologies, tools, and ways of working.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Costigan materially extends the cluster’s emphasis on shared knowledge infrastructure and selective adaptation by proposing firm-owned, curated knowledge graphs that convert accumulated documents and matter history into reusable organisational capacity. He also directly advances the release-chasing proposition by enabling firms to build applications on their own data rather than follow vendor roadmaps, although these benefits remain product claims rather than reported performance findings.
qs: I’ll start by saying our platform turns a firm’s documents and matter history into a private, curated knowledge graph that the firm owns and runs inside its own environment.
It takes firms away from having to follow the vendor roadmap and allows them to start building differentiated products for their firm immediately.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Costigan accepts the cluster’s claim that AI-enabled knowledge systems will pressure billable-hour and leverage-based economics, and materially extends it by identifying ownership of accumulated firm knowledge as the asset driving that shift. His account remains predictive and does not address verification, buyer incentives or the apprenticeship problem.
qs: The biggest shift is that a firm’s accumulated knowledge stops being a byproduct and becomes its most leveraged asset.
That really breaks the math on which the billable hour rests.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: Costigan concretely extends the cluster’s implementation focus by proposing that existing knowledge-management staff curate private-AI environments while agentic systems automate much of the infrastructure burden. This supports the view that advantage lies in organisational knowledge and delivery capacity rather than model access alone, though the evidence is an organisational self-report rather than demonstrated service-quality or staffing outcomes.
qs: I think existing knowledge management roles can be adapted to the curation and management of that aspect of the environment.
It is an agent environment where pretty much everything in our infrastructure is managed automatically, in a highly governed way.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source accepts the need for careful implementation and materially extends it by identifying two concrete selection and adoption priorities: preserving firm control over AI infrastructure and giving users agency during workplace change. Its product claims and leadership advice are experiential rather than outcome-tested.
qs: Every AI tool asked a firm to choose between productivity and control.

I think it is a good thing for leaders to remember at this time, and something for all of us to remember as we encourage people to change the way they work and adopt new technologies, tools, and ways of working.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model and materially extends it with a concrete infrastructure design: firm-owned knowledge graphs and ontologies, private deployment, agent-led curation, cited outputs, model-based checking and retained human review. Its accuracy, maintenance, staffing and pricing claims remain vendor assertions or predictions rather than independently demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Stephen Costigan (15:00)  What I mean is that the system is not there to replace a lawyer’s judgment.

I would say the firm needs to define and approve the ontology for practice areas and maintain a light human-in-the-loop review queue, where the system can flag lower-confidence data extractions before they are committed to the graph.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Costigan supports the cluster’s core mechanism by predicting that curated knowledge infrastructure will compress routine associate work and reduce junior leverage. He adds a firm-economics and competitive-differentiation rationale, but does not directly address succession, apprenticeship, or proposed training responses.
qs: When that precedent becomes a curated graph, routine production work compresses dramatically.
The firms that own that graph will deliver senior judgment with far less junior leverage.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Costigan supports the cluster’s proposition that legal AI value depends on firm-specific context, knowledge infrastructure and implementation rather than model capability alone. His firm-owned, internally hosted knowledge graph also supports the cluster’s emphasis on data control and competing integration architectures, though he provides product claims rather than measured performance evidence.
qs: I’ll start by saying our platform turns a firm’s documents and matter history into a private, curated knowledge graph that the firm owns and runs inside its own environment.
It then puts research, drafting, review, and enterprise search on top of that graph.

kp.k: Knowledge graphs encode relationships missing from document similarity
kp.d: Costigan argues that legal knowledge graphs connect clients, matters, parties, clauses and obligations rather than merely retrieving similar text. He presents Atlas AI as converting internal documents and matter histories into firm-owned infrastructure supporting research, drafting, review and enterprise search.
qs: A knowledge graph is the opposite. It is a map of your knowledge where the things that matter, clients, matters, parties, clauses, and obligations, are represented as connected entities.
It captures the relationships, not only the text to which it refers.
It then puts research, drafting, review, and enterprise search on top of that graph.

kp.k: Firm ontologies allegedly improve grounding beyond hybrid retrieval
kp.d: Costigan asserts that combining traditional search, vector search and knowledge graphs still falls short of legal accuracy requirements. He attributes substantial accuracy improvements in drafting and enterprise search to incorporating the firm's ontology into the index and using agents to map data; he supplies no numerical accuracy results or test methodology.
qs: Even with traditional search, adding vector search, adding a knowledge graph, and bringing all of those together into a hybrid search pipeline, you are still not going to achieve the level of accuracy that law requires.
We bring the firm’s ontology into the index, its information architecture, if you will, in a traditional way of describing it, and then use agents to map that data.
At a high level, that is what we are doing, and that is why we are seeing big increases in accuracy when drafting and performing enterprise search.

kp.k: Automated curation shifts firms toward knowledge governance
kp.d: Costigan rejects the need for a year-long cleaning programme before AI delivers value. He says Atlas AI's Librarian continuously extracts entities and relationships, resolves duplicates and maps incoming iManage and SharePoint content to the firm's ontology. Firms retain responsibility for approving practice-area ontologies and reviewing lower-confidence extractions before graph inclusion, shifting their contribution from manual cleaning to judgment.
qs: They assume a year-long data-cleaning program is necessary before any value is derived. That is not really the case anymore.
It resolves duplicates, reconciles the same party appearing in different forms, and maps everything to the firm’s ontology.

I would say the firm needs to define and approve the ontology for practice areas and maintain a light human-in-the-loop review queue, where the system can flag lower-confidence data extractions before they are committed to the graph.

kp.k: Private deployment reframes confidentiality as architectural control
kp.d: Costigan contrasts reliance on SaaS vendors' contractual assurances with deployment inside the firm's Azure environment under firm-controlled keys. He claims the data, graph, embeddings and audit trail remain within that environment and models operate under zero-data-retention terms without third-party training. He presents this configuration as enabling demonstrable data flows and use on sensitive matters; these are vendor architectural and governance claims.
qs: It is changing confidentiality from a promise into an architecture.
But with Atlas AI, the platform runs inside the firm’s own Azure environment under the firm’s keys. The data, the graph, the embeddings, and the audit trail, none of it leaves the firm’s environment.
The models are accessed under zero-data-retention terms, so nothing is retained and nothing trains a third party’s system.

kp.k: Agentic workflows move lawyers from assembly to judgment
kp.d: Costigan describes an augmentation model: diligence workflows generate checklists or issues lists with subsection-level citations, while bulk contract review produces source-traceable answers across hundreds of documents. A separate model challenges the draft and citation precision before lawyer review. Although he calls this an adversarial verification step and a verified draft, the described checking is automated, with lawyers remaining responsible for editing and deciding; no measured reliability evidence accompanies the claim.
qs: What I mean is that the system is not there to replace a lawyer’s judgment. It is there to deliver a strong, cited first draft. The lawyer spends time editing and deciding, not assembling.
Every line item carries an inline citation to the exact subsection from which it came, not simply Section 3, but Section 3.2(a).

For bulk contract review, you define the question once, such as change of control, governing law, or termination, and the system extracts structured answers across hundreds of documents into a reviewable grid.
One model drafts, and a separate model is tasked with arguing against it, checking that the deliverable does what was asked and that every citation is precise.

kp.k: Owned knowledge infrastructure becomes the proposed competitive advantage
kp.d: Costigan argues that buying identical tools and datasets cannot sustain practice differentiation. He presents editable, firm-owned graphs that accumulate knowledge from successive matters as the defensible asset, while predicting commoditisation of the model layer. His contrast with centralised vendors includes the assertion that firms' knowledge improves vendors' systems rather than their own assets.
qs: My thoughts are, number one, you are not going to build a differentiated practice area in your firm or maintain differentiation by buying the same product and using the same data set as everyone else.
With our platform, or with private AI infrastructure in general, you build a curated graph that you own outright. That compounds with every matter you work on and bring into the platform.
First, the ontology is yours and editable. You govern how your knowledge is structured, not some vendor.
The model layer is becoming a commodity. The curated graph is part of the defensible asset, and it should belong to the firm.

kp.k: Infrastructure agents could reduce specialist staffing requirements
kp.d: Costigan predicts that existing knowledge-management roles can adapt to managing private AI infrastructure as agent-based management develops. He describes Atlas AI's Enclave as automating infrastructure management under governance and reports that the share of its platform written agentically rose from around 10 percent to 60 or 65 percent, without specifying a period. He uses this experience to argue that firms need not maintain large infrastructure teams, and agrees that Atlas AI users would not need to hire GPU deployment and monitoring professionals.
qs: I think existing knowledge management roles can be adapted to the curation and management of that aspect of the environment.
It is an agent environment where pretty much everything in our infrastructure is managed automatically, in a highly governed way.
When we look at the amount of code written agentically in our organization, we have gone from around 10 percent to 60 or 65 percent of our platform being written agentically.
Everyone thinks they are going to need a huge team to manage their own private infrastructure, but that is simply not the case anymore.

kp.k: Curated data enables firm-directed application development
kp.d: Costigan identifies automated document-management-system curation as particularly valuable for knowledge-management teams, which he describes as typically one to five people if fortunate. Beyond curation, he advocates enabling firms to build their own applications using Claude Code and Atlas AI's MCP access to curated data, reducing dependence on vendor feature roadmaps.
qs: Again, the team size is typically one to five people in that particular area of the firm, if they are lucky.
But I think what is critical is automating the curation of the DMS.
You can take Claude Code, for instance, use our MCP, access your curated data set, and build whatever applications you want, either separate from or integrated into our platform.
It takes firms away from having to follow the vendor roadmap and allows them to start building differentiated products for their firm immediately.

kp.k: Knowledge ownership could reshape leverage and hourly pricing
kp.d: In the explicitly predictive closing discussion, Costigan argues that curated precedents will compress routine production, enabling senior judgment with fewer junior fee earners and fixed-fee, on-demand client offerings. He predicts that effective knowledge ownership, rather than head count, will distinguish firms from competitors renting common tools and competing on price. His five-year outlook is a strategic forecast, not an observed staffing or pricing outcome.
qs: The traditional model monetizes leverage. Partners sell associate hours against precedents that live in people’s heads and scattered files today.
When that precedent becomes a curated graph, routine production work compresses dramatically.

The firms that own that graph will deliver senior judgment with far less junior leverage. They will be able to productize their expertise through fixed-fee, on-demand, client-facing offerings in ways the hourly model never allowed.
Firms that treat AI as a tool they rent will compete on price against everyone renting the same tools.

Just to land this point, in five years the question will not be which AI tool your firm uses. It will be whether your firm owns its knowledge or rents access to it from a bunch of knowledge providers.

kp.k: Adoption leadership should foster hope and personal agency
kp.d: In the opening contribution, Nikki Shaver reports lessons from a positive-psychology panel at the preceding week's FT Innovative Lawyers Summit in London. She recommends that leaders counter pessimism by offering hope, a pathway forward and personal agency, arguing that lawyers and employees are less likely to adopt new technologies and working methods without agency. This is reported panel advice and her recommendation, not a measured adoption finding.
qs: Do not let people sit in their little pockets of pessimism. It will spread.
First, create a sense of hope, then provide a vision for the way forward.
Then provide people with a sense that they have agency to drive that path forward.
They are much less likely to do so if they do not feel that they have agency themselves.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Stephen Costigan claims that private knowledge infrastructure improves legal AI accuracy, automates curation, changes lawyers’ production work, and creates firm-specific competitive advantage.
pts.d: Costigan, Atlas AI’s founder, describes a firm-owned knowledge graph linking clients, matters, documents, clauses and obligations. He claims that incorporating the firm’s ontology into the index and using agents to map data produces substantial accuracy gains beyond hybrid search alone. He says continuous automated curation reduces the need for manual precedent cleaning. He presents private deployment as an architectural protection for confidentiality, with firm-controlled infrastructure and zero-data-retention model access. For diligence and bulk contract review, he describes cited drafts and structured answers checked by a second, adversarial model before lawyers edit and decide; this is an augmentation claim, not replacement of lawyer judgment. His term 'adversarial verification' describes automated model checking, distinct from human verification. He further claims that agent-managed infrastructure reduces staffing requirements and that access to curated data enables firms to build applications rather than follow a vendor roadmap. His market prediction is that models become commodities while owned knowledge graphs become compounding assets, compressing routine production, reducing associate-to-partner leverage, enabling fixed-fee client-facing products, and distinguishing firms from competitors renting common tools.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists principally of Costigan’s enterprise-software experience, descriptions of Atlas AI’s architecture and workflows, and one internal coding statistic.
pts.d: Costigan grounds his account in years building enterprise software, predominantly in the AmLaw 50, and describes Atlas AI’s Librarian curation component, firm-hosted deployment, source-linked review grids and adversarial model checks. These are speaker-reported capabilities and mechanisms, not reported independent evaluations. His claim of large accuracy improvements includes no numerical accuracy results, benchmark methodology or named client outcomes. For reduced infrastructure staffing needs, he cites agent-based management and reports that the share of his company’s platform written agentically rose from around 10 percent to 60–65 percent; he supplies no measurement period or method, and the statistic concerns platform development rather than law-firm staffing outcomes. The claims about ownership, pricing, junior leverage and competitive winners and losers are strategic predictions, explicitly offered in the crystal-ball discussion, rather than findings supported by market data in this transcript.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Costigan presents most technical capabilities as available now, lower-burden infrastructure management as a near-future development, and ownership-led market differentiation on a five-year horizon.
pts.d: In the source labeled 2026, automated continuous curation, cited drafting, bulk review and firm-specific application development are presented as current capabilities. Accuracy depends on grounding in structured knowledge and incorporating the firm’s ontology; Costigan says hybrid search alone does not meet legal accuracy requirements. Firms must define and approve practice-area ontologies and retain a human review queue for low-confidence extractions. His confidentiality claim is tied to deployment in the firm’s Azure environment under its keys and model access under zero-data-retention terms. Reduced infrastructure-management burden is framed both as already emerging and as a near-future possibility through agents and adapted knowledge-management roles. Competitive advantage is conditional on firms owning, curating and effectively using their graphs, not ownership alone. The business-model discussion is forward-looking without a separate quantified schedule for production compression or reduced junior leverage; the final ownership-versus-rental prediction expressly uses five years, approximately 2031 if measured from the supplied source year.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are law firms, lawyers and associates, knowledge-management teams, firm governance personnel, clients and legal-AI vendors.
pts.d: Costigan speaks broadly about law firms, with his experience concentrated in elite AmLaw 50 enterprises. Lawyers conducting diligence, drafting and contract review would shift from assembly toward editing and judgment. Partners would deliver senior judgment with fewer junior fee earners relative to partners; he does not quantify job losses or hiring changes. Knowledge-management staff would move away from manual cleaning toward ontology governance, curation and infrastructure management, with agents limiting the need for a large specialist team. Firm general counsel and conflicts partners would gain visibility into data flows under the described private architecture. Clients are implicated through confidentiality protections and prospective fixed-fee, on-demand offerings, not an access-to-justice claim. Firms owning and using curated knowledge would, in his prediction, gain differentiated products and durable advantage, while firms renting common tools would face price competition. Legal-AI vendors are implicated by his claim that model-based tooling is becoming commoditized and that firm-owned knowledge infrastructure is the more durable market position.
